doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Honest criticism and Ruby Braff
summary: He avoids calling musicians idiots, hints at poor performances, and praises Ruby Braff, who objected to his Pizza Express piece.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: I don’t know, sometimes you read things and they make statements that mean everything and nothing. Like the “quintessential player.” And what is that exactly?

Yeah, well people say well what happens if someone has performed badly? It’s very difficult. I’m always interested in what the artistic pretensions are, or what the artistic intentions are. If an artist appears to be claiming a degree of significance and then fails to perform up to that degree of significance I will say so. But if an artist who I respect and who has made no such claims simply doesn’t perform very well I will find a way, as it were, of not saying that. I will try to find some way of saying something like the drummer’s contributions were not noteworthy. Or the drummer’s contributions neither added much nor detracted from the performance. You are damning with faint praise if you like. I don’t think it’s my role to say this man is an idiot. But I can leave something semi-said and someone will read between the lines.
Is there someone you hear frequently that in their own estimation of their playing is very unpretentious that you feel constantly rises to the occasion?

Well I think Ruby [Braff] is a good example of that, isn’t he? I think essentially that is what I’ve found so inspiring about him. But I’ve known Ruby a great many years now. And he never fails to find something special to say, yet I don’t think he’s trying to stand

up and say hang on, I’m of considerable artistic significance therefore please, you know, treat me in that sort of way. I’ll give you an example. I wrote a piece about him when he was appearing at Pizza Express in London, which is still a famous jazz club. And it’s a club where people come in to eat, and they make a lot of noise. They clatter and chatter and it’s the sort of place in the center of London where people come in to eat who have no interest really in whether it’s Ruby Braff or Vera Lynn. It’s just an incidental. And I don’t like that. And I wrote a long piece, you know which ended up with something like what a shame it was that the audience didn’t pay sufficient attention to music of this quality. And Ruby telephoned me. He said what were you saying all that in the article? I said well it’s what I believe. I said it’s a damn shame that they should have talked and clattered about. He said look hang on, I’m a saloon player. This is like a saloon. These guys are in a saloon. I’m a saloon player. I expect that kind of noise and chatter. I thought all right.
